title: Self-test: Vol I, Ch 3: ML Lifecycle

questions.prompt: Team A ships a DR screening model and freezes all development once the model clears validation in the lab, treating subsequent tasks as standard server operations. Team B treats launch as the beginning of an ongoing feedback loop, monitoring telemetry and data distributions to guide evidence-based updates. Which team's posture aligns with the chapter's lifecycle, and why?

options.label: Team B — the lifecycle is a closed loop where operational feedback and distribution drift continuously reshape upstream data and model decisions
Team A — once a model meets offline validation thresholds its statistical properties are fixed and need only infrastructure maintenance
Team A — updating a validated model in production introduces regulatory risk that outweighs drift adaptation
Team B — the lifecycle mandates automatic daily retraining regardless of whether distributions have drifted

questions.explanation: Deployment starts the feedback loop rather than ending the project: production inputs, demographics, and equipment shift even when code is untouched. Regulatory frameworks mandate lifecycle management and change control — not frozen models — and the lifecycle prescribes evidence-driven intervention, not unconditional retraining.

questions.prompt: An engineering team completes problem definition with clinical sensitivity targets but records the target deployment environment as 'TBD.' Which failure mode does this set up?

options.label: None — deployment can be chosen freely once accuracy is optimized
A late-discovery failure: the physical-layer constraint exists but was never bound, so downstream data and architecture decisions can harden around an infeasible target
Only a documentation gap, since monitoring will flag any memory overflow post-launch
A data-collection problem, because the paradigm choice determines which images are legally shareable

questions.explanation: Deployment paradigm is a stage-1 output that constrains every downstream stage — memory, latency, and data-residency requirements differ across cloud/edge/mobile/TinyML. The day-153 failure is exactly this: the 500 MB reservation existed from day one but was never written into a contract.

questions.prompt: Deployment discovers the trained model needs 4 GB while the clinic device reserves ~500 MB. Walking the stage-interface contracts back, which stage owns the defect?

options.label: Deployment — it found the defect, so it owns the fix
Model development — it chose an oversized architecture
Problem definition — the earliest boundary whose contract never stated the memory condition
Evaluation — it should have measured model size alongside sensitivity

questions.explanation: Ownership is assigned by which boundary should have recorded the condition, not by where it surfaced. Evaluation measured what its contract required (sensitivity); model development received no memory budget; problem definition handed off without the constraint — so the fix starts there.

questions.prompt: What is the primary conceptual distinction between model evaluation and model validation as the chapter defines them?

options.label: Evaluation uses the test set; validation uses the training set

Evaluation measures model behavior on chosen datasets and metrics; validation assembles the broader evidence — latency, subgroup floors, robustness, operational readiness, cost — needed for a specified deployment decision
Evaluation happens after deployment; validation happens before
They are synonyms for the same offline accuracy check

questions.explanation: Evaluation supplies measurements; validation is the release decision that consumes them plus system-level evidence. A model can pass every accuracy check and still fail validation on latency, subgroup reliability, or cost — validation cannot be reduced to 'one more test.'

questions.prompt: A DR model achieves 94% aggregate sensitivity on held-out validation data. How should the validation stage treat this number before release?

options.label: As sufficient evidence — 94% clears the 90% floor
As insufficient: aggregate numbers hide subgroup drops, so stratified evaluation across age brackets, conditions, and camera models must confirm no critical subgroup falls below its floor
As grounds to lower the classification threshold until aggregate sensitivity reaches 99%
As proof the deployment target is feasible

questions.explanation: The chapter's own example: 94% aggregate can conceal <80% sensitivity on cataract patients or low-light clinics — local failures invisible in the average that surface as missed diagnoses after launch. Release requires per-subgroup evidence in the manifest.

questions.prompt: In routine care, only flagged or borderline patients get specialist grading; patients the model cleared are never re-examined. What does this imply for measuring field sensitivity?

options.label: Nothing — referral outcomes provide all the labels needed
Field sensitivity is unmeasurable from routine outcomes: misses among cleared patients stay unseen unless the monitoring data path labels a sample of unreferred images
Sensitivity can be estimated from referral-rate changes alone
The model's training-set sensitivity applies indefinitely

questions.explanation: The routing policy creates a selection hole: false negatives produce no referral and therefore no label. The chapter's remedy is a dedicated monitoring data path — sampled images uploaded off-hours and graded centrally — which is also the retraining data source.

questions.prompt: Explain to a software-engineering colleague why 'the artifact is untouched but the model degraded' — no exception, no crash, silent accuracy loss — and why monitoring exists as a lifecycle stage because of it.
questions.modelAnswer: A traditional binary's behavior is a function of its code: unchanged code means unchanged behavior. An ML model's behavior is a function of code plus the distribution it learned — and the distribution is outside the artifact. When production inputs drift (new camera color profiles, demographic shifts), the learned features meet pixel distributions never sampled in training; accuracy falls while every unit test passes and the latency SLA holds. Monitoring exists because no conventional alarm can see this: statistical telemetry (drift tests, proxy signals, delayed labeled outcomes) is the only sensor pointed at the thing that actually changed. The degradation equation formalizes it — accuracy tracks divergence between production and training data, not code version.

questions.prompt: A team treats its held-out test set as the model-selection signal, retraining until a candidate finally clears it. Explain what this does to the evidence the release decision relies on.
questions.modelAnswer: The test set's evidentiary value comes from its independence: it measures a model it didn't shape. Using it to select is fitting by proxy — each rejection-and-retry leaks information about the test distribution into the search, so the 'held-out' score becomes optimistically biased, a mild form of overfitting to the test set itself. Validation then inherits corrupted evidence: the one number meant to bound generalization can no longer bound anything. The fix is role separation — a validation set for selection, the test set touched once for the release manifest, and fresh or rotating evaluation data if selection must continue.

questions.prompt: A validation pipeline clears one release candidate per week; a rebuilt pipeline clears one per day. Over a 26-week window, how many candidates does each clear, and what is the search-breadth ratio?
questions.modelAnswer: N = T_window / t_cycle. Weekly: 26 weeks / 1 week = 26 candidates. Daily: 26 × 7 = 182 candidates. Ratio ≈ 182/26 = 7× — the same iteration-tax arithmetic as the book's ~3.8× (hourly vs weekly training), scaled to the validation boundary. The tax applies at every slow stage, not just training: whichever boundary cycles slowest caps the whole loop's learning rate.

questions.prompt: A screening program submits 1,838 clinic images; 393 come back ungradable. What share is rejected, and at 100 patients/day how many unscreened patients does that rate produce weekly?
questions.modelAnswer: f_reject = 393/1838 ≈ 0.214, about 21% — the Beede 2020 field result. At 100 patients/day the program rejects ~21 patients/day unscreened, or ~150 per week (~147 exactly at 21.4%). This is why image-quality checks move to capture time: a rejected image discovered at inference is a patient sent home.
